question: None shared. P-114 (Seifallahi et al., the gait/ANFIS paper the ledger means, present in the pack as pdf/P-115.txt; pack pdf/P-114.txt is P-112's EEG paper) separates MCI from healthy controls using Kinect gait (the gait/motor channel). P-5 classifies AD/MCI/CN three ways from fundus photographs and OCT (the eye/retina channel). The measurement channels differ, and so does the contrast (binary vs three-class).
metric: Mismatch: binary accuracy (93%) vs the MCI-class precision (positive predictive value, 84.96%) of a three-class model.

figures.P-114: Binary MCI vs HC, ANFIS on all dual-task gait features: accuracy 93%, sensitivity 90%, F-score 91.5% (n = 150: 70 MCI, 80 HC; the ANFIS evaluation protocol is not stated). Wilson with n = 150: 0.878-0.961.
figures.P-5: First dataset (29 MCI, 50 CN, 38 AD patients; image-level 5-fold CV): three-class accuracy 91.64%, AUC 96.78%; MCI-class precision 84.96%. Second dataset (nCI vs pCI by MMSE/MoCA): accuracy 82.46%. No binary MCI-vs-CN accuracy. No interval arithmetic was done because no shared quantity exists.

matched_figure_check: No matched figure is possible: P-5 reports no binary MCI-vs-CN accuracy, and P-114 reports no retinal result.
performance_validity: Passes: no contested figure reaches 0.97 (P-5's AUC is 96.78%; P-114's 99% specificity is not the compared figure).
reason: The two studies measure different channels (Kinect gait vs retinal imaging) and different contrasts (binary MCI vs HC vs a per-class figure from an AD/MCI/CN model). The compared numbers are also different statistics (accuracy vs class precision). This is the same pair as C-29.

quotes.quote: the proposed ANFIS classifier had values of 93%, 90%, and 91.5% for accuracy, sensitivity, and F-score, respectively when all extracted gait parameters in the DTW condition for the classification of elderly subjects to MCI and HC groups.
novel method is presented to detect MCI among elders from skeletal data of elders’ gait recorded with a Kinect.
Of 150 selected subjects, 80 subjects were healthy individuals without any cognitive impairments (HC subjects), and 70 subjects were elderly people with MCI.
The proposed method achieved high precision rates of 84.96% and 80.90% in classifying MCI and positive test scores for cognitive impairment, respectively.
The neural network was applied to classify individuals with MCI, Alzheimer’s disease, and control participants with normal cognition.
As shown in Table 2, the proposed network DuCAN had an accuracy of 91.64% and an AUC of 96.78%.
